title: Shield Platform Encryption, field audit trail, event monitoring, and transaction security overview
objectives: Place Shield Platform Encryption, Field Audit Trail, Event Monitoring, and Transaction Security as complementary Shield-family controls, not as substitutes for CRUD, FLS, or sharing.
Explain encryption as protecting data at rest, audit trail as field-history retention, event monitoring as activity visibility, and transaction security as policy reactions to events.
Refuse invented retention years, event counts, or edition gates; mark them Needs verification in current Help and the org.
Choose which control matches a compliance story: rest encryption, who-changed-the-field, who-exported-the-report, or block-this-action.
diagnostic_question: A regulator asks four things: SSN at rest must be encrypted, Amount history must be retained beyond ordinary field history, report exports must be visible, and mass-export from an unusual IP should be blocked. Which Shield-family control is each, and which ordinary security gate still applies first?
definition: Salesforce Shield is a suite of add-on security products. Shield Platform Encryption encrypts data at rest in Salesforce while remaining distinct from Classic Encryption. Field Audit Trail extends field-history style auditing for compliance (confirm current Help for what it stores and how long). Event Monitoring provides event log visibility into user and system activity such as logins and report exports. Transaction Security (including enhanced/real-time policies) evaluates events and can notify or block. These products require appropriate licenses; they do not replace object permissions, FLS, or record sharing. ([Platform Encryption](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_pe_overview.htm); [Field Audit Trail](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.field_audit_trail.htm); [Event Monitoring](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.event_monitoring.htm))
why_it_matters: Teams buy encryption expecting it to hide Amount from sales, or they skip FLS because Event Monitoring exists. Interviewers want the split: encryption is not authorization, audit is not a block, monitoring is not encryption, transaction security is not a sharing rule. Inventing '10 years' or '70 events' without Help is a fail.
sixty_second_explanation: Think of a bank vault room. Platform Encryption is locking the vault steel so disks in the data center are unreadable if stolen—tellers with permission still work at the window. Field Audit Trail is the numbered ledger of who changed a balance field. Event Monitoring is the camera tape of who walked in and who printed a report. Transaction Security is the guard who can stop a suspicious bag at the door. None of those replaces the teller's badge (CRUD/FLS) or which drawers they may open (sharing).
deeper_explanation: Shield Platform Encryption protects data at rest. It is not the same as Classic Encryption. You select data elements through encryption policy (fields, files, and other elements described in current Help). Key management, including Bring Your Own Key where entitled, is part of the product. Encryption does not replace FLS: a user with field access still sees decrypted values in the app. Confirm field types that support encryption in the implementation guide/Help; do not invent a list. ([Platform Encryption](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_pe_overview.htm))

Standard Field History Tracking is not Field Audit Trail. FAT is the Shield capability for longer-term, compliance-oriented field history. Retention periods, objects, and storage are license- and configuration-specific. Quote current Field Audit Trail Help rather than marketing pages. ([Field Audit Trail](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.field_audit_trail.htm))

Event Monitoring captures event types (logins, API, report export, and others listed in current Help). It is visibility and forensics, not a default block. Real-Time Event Monitoring is a related capability; confirm which SKU the org has. Do not invent an event-type count. ([Event Monitoring](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.event_monitoring.htm))

Transaction Security policies can react to events (for example block or alert) using clicks or Apex depending on the policy type documented for the org. It is not OWD and not FLS. License and which events are eligible are Needs verification. ([Transaction Security](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_transaction.htm))
Ordinary gates still come first: authentication, user permissions, object/FLS, sharing. Shield sits on top for regulated data, audit, and monitoring.

Classic Encryption is a different, narrower feature; do not equate it to Shield.

interview_explanation.two_minutes: I map the regulator's sentence to a product: rest, history, visibility, reaction. I refuse numbers I cannot cite from Help. I say Classic Encryption is not Shield. I say monitoring without a policy does not block. I keep least privilege on permission sets. If the org lacks Shield, I say so instead of designing fake policies.

terminology.plain: Encrypts selected Salesforce data while it is stored.
terminology.precise: Policy-driven at-rest encryption with Salesforce-managed or customer-managed keys where entitled. Distinct from Classic Encryption.
terminology.example: Encrypt LAB_SSN__c at rest after confirming the field type is supported.
terminology.non_example: Hiding Amount from a salesperson who still has FLS read.
terminology.boundary: Functional limitations per field type: read Help, do not invent.

terminology.plain: An older, narrower encryption feature, not the Shield product.
terminology.precise: Help distinguishes Classic Encryption from Shield Platform Encryption. Do not treat them as interchangeable.
terminology.example: A legacy encrypted custom field that is not Shield policy encryption.
terminology.boundary: Availability Needs verification; do not claim it exists in every org.

terminology.plain: Shield-grade history of field changes for compliance.
terminology.precise: Extends beyond ordinary Field History Tracking. Retention and setup are in Field Audit Trail Help—do not invent a year count.
terminology.example: Retain Amount changes for a regulated object after FAT is entitled and configured.
terminology.non_example: Standard 20-field history on an object without FAT (do not invent the 20 if you cannot cite it here—Needs verification of standard FHT limits).
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Event Monitoring: actions, not necessarily field old/new values.
terminology.boundary: Standard Field History Tracking is a separate setup.

terminology.plain: Logs of what users and integrations did.
terminology.precise: Event log visibility (and related real-time products where licensed) for types documented in Help, such as logins and report exports.
terminology.example: Investigate who exported a LAB report.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Transaction Security: can act on events, not only store them.

terminology.plain: Policies that react to events—alert or block as configured.
terminology.precise: Evaluates selected events and takes documented policy actions. Enhanced/real-time variants depend on SKU.
terminology.example: Block a report export event type if Help lists it as eligible and the org is entitled.

terminology.plain: Data sitting in storage, not currently being typed in a browser.
terminology.precise: The state Platform Encryption is designed to protect in Salesforce data centers.
terminology.non_example: TLS in transit (a different control family).
terminology.confusable_neighbor: FLS: authorization to see the value when using the app.
terminology.boundary: In-transit encryption is not this product's headline.

interview_questions.question: Give a Shield overview without inventing limits.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Platform Encryption is at rest. Field Audit Trail is field-change history. Event Monitoring is activity logs. Transaction Security can block or alert. Licenses Need verification. None replaces FLS or sharing.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I map sentences, not SKU folklore. Rest, ledger, camera, guard. I distinguish Classic Encryption. I say monitoring is not a block. I keep CRUD/FLS/sharing first. If asked for 10 years or 70 events I open Help instead of guessing. That honesty is the interview-ready close.
interview_questions.example: Four regulator asks mapped to four products plus FLS for SSN in the UI.
tradeoffs: Buy Shield vs tighten ordinary security first

interview_questions.question: Why is encryption not field-level security?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Encryption protects stored bytes. Users who are authorized still see decrypted values in the app. Hiding Amount is FLS (and maybe layout, which is weaker).
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I tell the stolen-disk versus salesperson story. Platform Encryption is for the disk. FLS is for the person. You often need both: FLS so sales cannot see SSN, encryption so a storage compromise is less catastrophic. I mention possible filter/search limitations from Help after encryption. I do not turn off FLS because encryption is on.
interview_questions.example: LAB_AE_East still must lack SSN FLS after LAB_SSN__c is encrypted.
tradeoffs: Functional impact of encryption vs residual UI risk
Who is allowed to see decrypted values

interview_questions.question: Regulator wants report-export visibility and a block on a suspicious export pattern. Design?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Event Monitoring for visibility. Transaction Security for a block if the event is eligible and licensed. Least-privilege export permissions still first. Not OWD.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: Situation: data loss worry. Task: see and maybe stop. Action: shrink who has export user permissions, enable Event Monitoring if entitled, add a Transaction Security policy only after Help lists the event. Test in disposable org. Result: we can answer who exported, and we only claim a block if the SKU and event match. I will not promise a number of event types.
interview_questions.example: LAB report export in logs; policy only if Setup shows an eligible event.
tradeoffs: Block false positives vs data loss
follow_ups: What if Transaction Security is missing?

interview_questions.question: They want Amount history for years. Standard Field History is already on. What do you say?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Standard Field History is not Field Audit Trail. FAT is the Shield product for extended auditing. I will read FAT Help for retention instead of quoting a blog.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I inspect whether FAT is entitled. If not, I present a gap: ordinary history may not meet the regulation. I do not invent 10 years. I also check which objects/fields FAT supports in Help. Encryption and FAT are complementary, not substitutes. Result: a written gap or a Help-cited retention design, never a marketing number in the SOW.
interview_questions.example: Opportunity Amount: FHT on versus FAT not licensed—Needs verification recorded.
tradeoffs: Buy FAT vs accept shorter history
follow_ups: How do you report on FAT?

interview_questions.question: Users cannot filter on a newly encrypted field. Diagnose.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Check Help limitations for that encrypted field type. This may be expected. Do not decrypt production to 'fix reports' without a design review. Confirm encryption was even the right control versus FLS.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: Situation: report breakage after encryption. Task: separate expected limitation from misconfiguration. Action: field type versus supported list, deterministic encryption options if Help describes them for that use case—without inventing option names. If they only needed UI hide, FLS would have avoided the filter loss. Result: either an accepted limitation, a Help-supported encryption scheme, or a rollback in the lab.
interview_questions.example: LAB custom text field encrypted; list view filter fails as documented.
tradeoffs: Deterministic vs probabilistic schemes if Help offers them
follow_ups: Can we encrypt a different field?

interview_questions.question: How do you place Shield on the security access path?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: After authentication and authorization: encryption wraps stored data, FAT records field changes, monitoring records actions, transaction security may intercept actions. Sharing still decides rows.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I would not start an access-path interview with Shield. Login, permissions, FLS, OWD, then Shield overlays. Guest Experience Cloud is still guest sharing rules, not encryption. Apex without sharing is still a leak path encryption will not fix in the UI. That sequencing shows architecture judgment.
interview_questions.example: SEC-010-style walk: LAB_AE_East FLS, then encrypt SSN, then monitor exports.
tradeoffs: Defense in depth vs overlapping tools
Cost of SKUs vs ordinary least privilege

interview_questions.question: Leadership bought Event Monitoring and still had a data leak via a permission set. What failed?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Monitoring without least privilege. Logs do not prevent a user who already has export and object access. Transaction Security or removing the permission would have been the control, plus FLS/sharing.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: Situation: cameras without locks. Task: fix authorization. Action: who had export, object Read, and broad sharing. Tighten permission sets, consider a policy if eligible, keep monitoring for after-the-fact. Result: we stop treating Event Monitoring as a sharing model. I would still use the logs to see what left.
interview_questions.example: LAB_Analyst had export plus too much object access; logs showed the export after the fact.
tradeoffs: Policy false positives vs open exports
follow_ups: Which user permission is export? (verify name in org)
weak_answer_warnings: Blaming Shield for not being FLS

interview_questions.question: Teach the vault-room analogy, then break it, and refuse invented numbers.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Steel is encryption, ledger is FAT, cameras are Event Monitoring, guard is Transaction Security, teller badge is FLS. It breaks when encrypted fields lose filters, when logs are not real-time, and when Classic Encryption is confused with Shield.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I walk the regulator through four rooms. I then say the teller still sees cash with a badge. I refuse 10 years and 70 events. I say SKUs Need verification. Close: ordinary Salesforce security still comes first.
interview_questions.example: Four asks, four products, FLS for SSN, no blog numbers on the whiteboard.
